title: Pride in practice
hookLine: the danger of feeling holier than others
tomorrow: a group chat is rating girls' looks. what does Simran do?

lines: A GIRL ON HER PHONE IN KIRTAN.
cards: Simran hasn't missed her morning Nitnem in a long run of days. She keeps a little tracker, and she's quietly proud of it.

Then at the gurdwara she notices a girl from school scrolling her phone all through kirtan, and a thought arrives before she can stop it: at least I take this seriously. She doesn't like that thought.
Later she tells Maya about the tracker, and Maya, who keeps no count of anything, asks an honest question: wait, is counting your prayers a good thing or a bad thing?

teach.h: VIEW TWO: A COUNT BECOMES A SCORE.
teach.b: The first view: keep the count. Nitnem is a discipline, and a tracker is just a way to keep a promise to yourself. Its best case: devotion that runs on mood comes and goes, and a simple record helps it stay.
The second view: count lightly, or not at all. Once practice has a number, it can become a score, and a score wants someone to beat. Its best case: Gurbani warns about exactly that.
In the Sukhmani, on ang 278, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds keeps wandering, birth after birth.

teach.h: ANG 278 AND 266: THE LOWLY ARE HIGH.
teach.b: And on ang 266, in paraphrase: whoever knows himself to be lowly is counted the highest of all. Both sides agree on what matters most.
The danger isn't the tracker; it's the thought Simran had about the girl with the phone. The practice that was meant to soften her made her feel above someone.
That's pride in practice, and it's sneaky, because it dresses up as devotion. It doesn't feel like pride from the inside. It feels like taking things seriously.
Simran keeps the tracker, for now; she's still deciding.
But after kirtan she finds out the girl's grandmother is in the hospital. The phone was the family group chat, with updates. Simran goes and sits next to her, and doesn't mention the tracker.
Some days, devotion looks like a phone.

how: Nitnem is the daily set of Sikh prayers; some Sikhs track their practice and some prefer not to, and Gurbani's warnings against spiritual pride are read by both.

o: taking honest pleasure in a daily routine
doubting whether your prayers are working
feeling holier than others because of your devotion

games.q: pride in practice — tap the pairs.
p: a count can become a score
calling yourself a doer of good deeds
the one who knows himself lowly

s: the more you practice, the less you can fall into pride
pride in practice is sneaky because it dresses up as devotion; the practice itself can feed it.
Guru Arjan writes that whoever knows himself to be lowly is counted highest
Sikhs all agree that tracking your prayers is wrong
Sikhs answer it two ways; both agree the danger is feeling above someone else.

games.q: your friend says keeping a streak of your daily reading is pride. you think it keeps you honest. what's the best case for your friend's side?
o: once practice has a number, it can turn into a score to beat.
real devotion shouldn't need any discipline at all.
a streak proves you're more devoted than others.
games.why: that's the second view's best case, and Gurbani backs the worry (ang 278). the first view's: devotion that runs on mood comes and goes.

practice: Think of someone whose devotion you admire, in any tradition or none: a grandparent who prays, a friend who volunteers, a neighbor who never skips a morning walk.
In your mind, write them one honest line of praise for it, and hold that line as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Pride in practice. Feeling holier than someone else, the thief that dresses up as devotion.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Nitnem, the daily set of Sikh prayers.

carryVoice: No holier than others: the one who knows himself lowly is counted high. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 278 (Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala 5, ashtpadi 12: aapas kau karamvant kahaavai, janam marai bahu jon bhramaavai), paraphrased
Ang 266 (Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala 5: aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa), paraphrased
